TOB.name: Tobit
TOB.sources: Composed in Aramaic or Hebrew (Qumran fragments found in both); set in Assyrian exile but written in the Diaspora, probably eastern Mediterranean.
TOB.summary: A Diaspora wisdom tale about the righteous Tobit, blinded by bird droppings while burying the dead, and his son Tobias, who travels to Media guided by the angel Raphael in disguise. Tobias marries Sarah, whose seven previous husbands were killed by the demon Asmodaeus. The book celebrates almsgiving, proper burial, prayer, and endogamy — marrying within Israel — as the pillars of faithful Diaspora life.

T01.note: Only the God of Israel is worshipped (1:4–6), but a heavenly court of named angels stands under him — Raphael is "one of the seven" (12:15).

T02.note: Endogamy within the tribe is commanded (4:12–13) and Jewish identity in exile is kept through burial and food laws; yet the nations will finally turn to God (14:6).

T03.note: The plot is orchestrated from the outset: Tobit's and Sarah's prayers are heard at the same moment and Raphael is sent to both (3:16–17).

T04.note: Tobit suffers despite his righteousness, but the book restores him in full: almsgiving "saves from death" (12:9) and the righteous are vindicated.

T05.note: Almsgiving and care for the poor (ethical) and proper burial and dietary purity (ritual) are co-equal obligations.

T06.note: A demon, Asmodeus, kills Sarah's husbands (3:8) and is bound by Raphael (8:3) — evil acting outside God. But Tobit says of his blindness, "he afflicted me, and he has had mercy" (11:15).

T07.note: Death leads to an "eternal place" and Hades (3:6; 13:2); no resurrection. Hope is for a long life, descendants and Jerusalem's restoration.

T08.note: Sarah is given in marriage by her father as a matter of law (7:10–13); Anna earns the household's income and argues back (2:11–14). The household is patriarchal.

T09.note: Works strongly emphasized: almsgiving "delivers from death and purges every sin" (12:9), burial of the dead, prayer — deeds of piety accumulate merit.

T10.note: Exile is punishment for sin, but "he will again have mercy" if Israel turns back (13:5–6). Conditional, with return always open.

T11.note: Providence governs: Sarah "was set apart for you before the world was made" (6:18). Human piety still matters.

T12.note: Tobit alone went to Jerusalem instead of the northern shrines (1:4–6) — the centralized ideal — but in exile piety is personal: prayer, alms, burial.

T14.note: Israel is scattered for its sins but God's chosen people will be gathered and Jerusalem glorified (ch. 13). Mostly privilege.

T15.note: Raphael's name means "God heals": the book is about healing (Tobit's eyes, Sarah's curse) and mercy after affliction.

T16.note: A folktale with demon, magic fish organs and the Ahikar legend, set in a garbled Assyrian history (1:15, 14:15).

T17.note: Tobit keeps the law of Moses meticulously — tithes, food laws, burial (1:6–11). The law is fixed and inherited.

T18.note: The story of two households, but Tobit prays not to be punished "for my sins and those of my ancestors" (3:3–5) and his hope is collective.

T19.note: The final prophecy (14:5–7) anticipates the rebuilt Temple, Israel's return and the conversion of the nations "when the times are fulfilled".

T20.note: Tobit's suffering is a trial of a righteous man, not retribution; the exile, though, is framed as punishment for the nation's sins (13:5).

conduct.diet: Tobit refuses to eat the food of the Gentiles when deported to Nineveh (1:10–13), maintaining dietary distinctiveness as a mark of Jewish identity in exile. Food purity is a non-negotiable boundary.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Endogamy is the book's central social ethic: Tobit charges Tobias to marry only within their tribe and family (4:12–13). Tobias's marriage to Sarah — arranged through the angel and conducted with prayer — is the narrative climax, presented as the model of proper covenantal marriage.
conduct.slavery: Household servants are assumed as normal social fixtures but are not the subject of ethical reflection.
conduct.economic_justice: Almsgiving is Tobit's defining virtue: 'Give some of your food to the hungry and some of your clothing to the naked. Give all your surplus as alms' (1:16–17; 4:7–11). The book presents generosity to the poor as the foundation of righteousness.
conduct.violence_war: Not addressed. The only violence in the book is the demon Asmodaeus, overcome by fish liver smoke — a supernatural rather than human conflict.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Tobit observes pilgrimage festivals, brings firstfruits and tithes to Jerusalem (1:6–8), and prays at set times (3:11). Proper burial is treated as a sacred obligation even at personal risk.

JDT.name: Judith
JDT.sources: Composed in Hebrew (now lost); the story is historically anachronistic (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria) and was likely never intended as literal history. Qumran yielded no fragments.
JDT.summary: A fictional heroic tale in which the pious widow Judith saves Israel by seducing the Assyrian general Holofernes, decapitating him while he sleeps, and returning his head to her city. The book celebrates female courage, ritual piety, and God's use of the humble and weak to defeat the arrogant powerful.

T01.note: Fierce exclusive monotheism: Holofernes' demand that Nebuchadnezzar alone be worshipped (3:8) is the blasphemy; "we know no other god but him" (8:20).

T02.note: Israel versus the nations; Holofernes embodies Gentile arrogance. Achior the Ammonite is circumcised and joins Israel (14:10) — the one opening.

T03.note: God cannot be tested or bound to a deadline: Judith rebukes the elders' five-day ultimatum (8:12–17). Not fickle, not foolable.

T04.note: Achior states the Deuteronomic rule: Israel is defeated only when it sins (5:17–21). The plot confirms it.

T05.note: Judith's piety is ritually exact — fasting, sackcloth, ablutions, kosher food in the enemy camp (12:2–9) — alongside ethical courage.

T06.note: No Satan; the enemy is human. God is "putting us to the test, as he did our ancestors" (8:25–27).

T07.note: No afterlife hope for Israel; Judith dies old and is mourned (16:23–24). But the enemy nations face "fire and worms" forever on the day of judgment (16:17).

T08.note: Judith acts alone, rebukes the male elders, keeps her estate and refuses remarriage (16:22). Her weapons are beauty and deception, but her agency is the book's point.

T09.note: Prayer and trust that God will act, and the courageous deed itself, are both essential; the deed decides.

T10.note: Conditional: protection depends on not having sinned or turned to idols (5:17–21; 8:18–20).

T11.note: Judith's free initiative drives the plot, though she frames it as "the Lord will deal with Israel by my hand" (8:33).

T12.note: The Jerusalem high priest and council direct the defense (4:6–8; 15:8); Judith dedicates the spoils at the Temple (16:18–20).

T13.note: Priestly leadership in Jerusalem frames events, but decisive authority passes to a lay widow who overrules the town elders.

T14.note: Election as protection: God defends his people and takes vengeance on the nations that rise against them (16:17).

T15.note: "The Lord is a God who crushes wars" (16:2), and the beheading is celebrated as his act. He is also "God of the lowly, helper of the oppressed" (9:11).

T16.note: Presented as literal narrative, but deliberately impossible: Nebuchadnezzar rules the Assyrians from Nineveh (1:1). A historical fiction.

T17.note: The law is kept scrupulously as given; Judith's observance is fixed even in the enemy camp.

T18.note: Israel is saved as a people; Judith is the instrument and the victory belongs to the community.

T19.note: Victory is this-worldly and immediate, though the closing hymn invokes a day of judgment on the nations (16:17).

T20.note: Israel's suffering is a test "as he did Abraham" (8:25–27), explicitly not punishment, since this generation has not worshipped idols (8:18–20).

conduct.diet: Judith brings her own food into Holofernes' camp — ritually pure provisions she has prepared herself (10:5; 12:2–4) — and refuses to eat from the general's table. Dietary distinctiveness is a mark of holiness even when one's life is at stake.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Judith is a model widow who refuses remarriage despite many suitors (16:22). Her sexual virtue — she uses her beauty as a weapon while maintaining absolute chastity — is central to her identity as a holy woman. Holofernes' lust is his fatal vulnerability.
conduct.slavery: Judith has a trusted female slave (maid) who accompanies her on the mission (8:10; 10:5). Slavery is assumed as normal; no ethical reflection on it.
conduct.clothing: Judith's deliberate dressing in fine clothes and jewelry to attract Holofernes (10:3–4) is presented as a weapon of holy strategy, not vanity. Her appearance is part of her arsenal.
conduct.economic_justice: Not specifically addressed. Judith is wealthy and acts from personal resources.
conduct.violence_war: The central act is targeted political assassination framed as holy war. Judith decapitates Holofernes with his own sword. The community then routs the leaderless army. Divine sanction for violence against Israel's enemies is explicit and celebrated.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Judith fasts on all days except sabbaths, new moons, and feast days (8:6). Her ritual calendar discipline is presented as part of her piety. She bathes ritually before entering Holofernes' camp.

AES.name: Additions to Esther
AES.sources: Six additions (A–F) inserted into the Greek translation of Esther to supply the explicit religiosity absent from the Hebrew original. Origin probably Alexandria.
AES.summary: Six sections added to the Greek Esther: Mordecai's dream, the king's decree ordering Jewish genocide, the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, Esther's audience with the king, the counter-decree, and Mordecai's dream interpretation. Together they supply God, prayer, and covenantal theology to what was a secular court tale.

T01.note: The additions supply God, absent from the Hebrew Esther: "you are Lord of all" (13:11); Esther abhors the gods of the nations (14:8–10).

T02.note: Intensifies the particularism: Esther "abhors the bed of the uncircumcised" and has not eaten at Haman's table (14:15–17).

T03.note: Mordecai's dream foretells everything and its interpretation ends "these things have come from God" (10:4). History is predetermined.

T04.note: Haman and the enemies are punished and the Jewish community is restored.

T05.note: Adds prayer, fasting, sackcloth and Esther's dietary observance at court to a politically savvy secular story.

T06.note: No supernatural evil; Haman is the human adversary (a dragon in Mordecai's dream).

T07.note: No afterlife. Deliverance in this life is everything.

T08.note: Esther prays and risks her life, but the additions make her faint before the king and have God change his spirit (15:7–8), muting the agency of the Hebrew Esther.

T09.note: The additions credit deliverance to prayer and God's action rather than Esther's plan.

T10.note: God chose Israel "as an everlasting inheritance" (13:15–17), but Esther confesses the exile came "because we glorified their gods" (14:6–7).

T11.note: God "made two lots" and remembered his people at the appointed time (10:10–12) — a strongly determinist frame.

T14.note: Election as privilege: one lot for the people of God, one for the nations (10:10).

T15.note: Deliverer of his people and destroyer of their enemies.

T16.note: Later literary additions: dream allegory, invented royal decrees, expanded prayers.

T17.note: The additions are themselves a revision of scripture — adding God, prayer and Torah observance to a book that lacked them.

T18.note: The fate of the Jewish community as a whole is at stake throughout.

T19.note: Mordecai's dream has cosmic dragons and nations massing for war, but it is fulfilled within the story.

T20.note: Esther's prayer: "we have sinned before you, and you have handed us over to our enemies" (14:6–7). Haman's plot itself is unjust persecution.

conduct.diet: Not specifically addressed in the additions, though Esther's prayer (Addition C) mentions she hates eating at the king's table and the food of the Gentiles — a detail absent from the Hebrew.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Esther's prayer (Addition C) reveals that she hates her marriage to an uncircumcised foreign king and has not eaten at his table. The additions make explicit what the Hebrew conceals: intermarriage with the Gentile king is a source of anguish, not triumph.
conduct.clothing: Esther puts on her royal robes before approaching the king — mentioned in both Hebrew and Greek versions as preparation for the dangerous audience.
conduct.violence_war: The counter-decree (Addition E) authorizes the Jews to defend themselves and kill their enemies on the appointed day. The additions frame this as divinely sanctioned self-defense.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Fasting and communal prayer (Addition C: Mordecai and Esther each pray) are the Jewish community's ritual response to the threat of genocide.

1MA.name: 1 Maccabees
1MA.sources: Written in Hebrew (now lost); Greek is the surviving form. A pro-Hasmonean dynastic history, probably composed in Jerusalem under John Hyrcanus I (135–104 BCE). The most historically reliable account of the Maccabean period.
1MA.summary: A historical chronicle of the Jewish revolt against Seleucid persecution from Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 BCE) through the early Hasmonean dynasty. Mattathias ignites the revolt; his son Judas Maccabeus leads the military campaigns and rededicates the Temple (Hanukkah, 164 BCE); his brothers Jonathan and Simon consolidate political and religious independence. God's role is implicit — there are no miracles; human courage and military strategy determine the outcome.

T01.note: Strict monotheism against the Hellenistic syncretism imposed by Antiochus — the defining conflict of the book.

T02.note: Jewish identity against assimilation is the whole stake; those who adopt Greek ways are traitors to be killed (2:23–26, 44).

T03.note: The most theologically restrained Maccabean text: God ("Heaven") is implicit and distant, never fickle but rarely seen.

T04.note: Fidelity and courage bring victory, but the faithful who refuse to fight on the Sabbath are slaughtered (2:29–38).

T05.note: Torah, circumcision, Sabbath, purity and the rededication of the Temple are what is defended; the Hasmoneans combine priestly and military roles.

T06.note: No supernatural evil; evil is Antiochus and the apostates.

T07.note: No afterlife: the dead heroes win "great honor and an everlasting name" (2:51) — survival in memory.

T08.note: Exclusively male heroes. Women appear as victims — mothers executed with their circumcised babies (1:60–61).

T09.note: Zeal for the law in action: fighting for Torah, observing it, rebuilding the Temple. Phinehas is the model (2:26, 54).

T10.note: Faithfulness is rewarded in history: "Abraham was found faithful... reckoned to him as righteousness" (2:52).

T11.note: Human agency drives everything: the Maccabees decide to fight, plan campaigns and win by their own courage. No angel tips the balance.

T12.note: The cleansing and rededication of the one Temple is the climax (4:36–59).

T13.note: Simon is made high priest and ruler "until a trustworthy prophet should arise" (14:41): priest-kings rule because prophecy has ceased.

T14.note: Election as an inheritance to defend; the chosen people's survival is the prize.

T15.note: Holy war: victory "comes from Heaven" (3:18–19), won through Judas's armies — the most extended theology of righteous warfare in the tradition.

T16.note: The most historically realistic text in the Apocrypha — dates, places, military details, minimal supernatural.

T17.note: The law adapts to survive: Mattathias decides to fight on the Sabbath rather than be wiped out (2:39–41).

T18.note: Israel as a national collective is the subject; individual heroes matter for the nation.

T19.note: No apocalypse; they wait for "a prophet to come" (4:46; 14:41) but expect no imminent end.

T20.note: Persecution is "very great wrath upon Israel" (1:64), yet martyrs die faithful; neither reading dominates.

conduct.diet: Antiochus's persecution specifically targets Jewish dietary laws: Jews are forced to eat pork and other unclean foods as a test of apostasy (1:47, 62–63). Many die rather than eat. Diet becomes a mortal marker of identity.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Not addressed specifically, though the Hasmonean dynasty's dynastic marriages are mentioned in passing.
conduct.slavery: Antiochus sells Jews into slavery (1:32). The Maccabees seek to free captives.
conduct.agriculture: The land lies fallow and uncultivated during the years of fighting and persecution (6:49, 53) — a sign of the land's suffering alongside the people.
conduct.economic_justice: Not directly addressed. The book's economic concern is with tribute, tribute refusal, and the resources needed for warfare.
conduct.violence_war: War is the central ethical subject: the Maccabees' decision to fight on the Sabbath after the slaughter of non-resisters (2:39–41) is among the most significant legal decisions in the book. Self-defense overrides Sabbath law — a practical ethics of survival.
conduct.ritual_calendar: The rededication of the Temple and institution of the eight-day festival of Hanukkah (4:36–59) is the book's climax. Proper Temple service — daily sacrifice, lampstand, incense, showbread — is restored. The Sabbath is a recurring point of conflict throughout.

2MA.name: 2 Maccabees
2MA.dating: c. 120 BCE (epitome); original five-volume work by Jason of Cyrene slightly earlier
2MA.sources: An epitome (condensation) of a now-lost five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene. More theologically reflective than 1 Maccabees, with explicit theology of martyrdom, resurrection, and divine intervention. Probably composed in Greek in the Diaspora.
2MA.summary: Covers the period from the high priest Onias III to Judas Maccabeus's defeat of Nicanor (180–161 BCE). Unlike 1 Maccabees, emphasizes divine miracles, angelic appearances, and the theology of martyrdom: those who die for the law will be resurrected. The seven brothers and their mother who die rather than eat pork (chapter 7) are the theological heart of the book and the earliest clear statement of bodily resurrection in Jewish literature.

T01.note: Strict monotheism against Hellenistic syncretism; God made the world "not out of things that existed" (7:28).

T02.note: God's special relationship with Israel and its Temple is the premise; Heliodorus and even Antiochus end up acknowledging Israel's God (3:35–39; 9:12–17).

T03.note: God governs history and disciplines Israel deliberately (6:12–16); epiphanies punctuate the narrative.

T04.note: Exact poetic justice: Jason, Menelaus and Antiochus each die a death that fits their crimes (5:9–10; 13:8; 9:5–28).

T05.note: Temple purity and festivals (the opening letters urge Hanukkah) alongside the martyrs' moral courage.

T06.note: No Satan: God sends the calamities to discipline his people (6:12–16).

T07.note: Bodily resurrection of the martyrs is explicit and central (7:9, 11, 14, 23, 29), and Judas prays for the dead in view of resurrection (12:43–45).

T08.note: The mother of the seven encourages her sons and dies last (7:20–41) — the book's strongest figure, praised for reinforcing "her woman's reasoning with a man's courage" (7:21).

T09.note: Keeping Torah to death is the defining act; Judas makes a sin offering for the dead (12:43).

T10.note: Punishment is swift but "he never withdraws his mercy from us" (6:16) — discipline within a covenant that holds.

T11.note: The martyrs choose to die rather than violate Torah — human choice is real — but divine intervention is also decisive.

T12.note: The one Temple is the center: its desecration, purification and the festivals that commemorate it frame the book.

T13.note: High priests are the key figures — the righteous Onias III against the corrupt Jason and Menelaus; no prophets.

T14.note: God punishes Israel quickly so its sins do not accumulate, unlike the nations he leaves to fill up theirs (6:12–16): election as severe privilege.

T15.note: Heavenly horsemen strike Heliodorus (3:25) and fight beside Judas (10:29–30).

T16.note: Historical framework, but epiphanies, legendary martyrdoms and Hellenistic rhetoric shape it.

T17.note: The martyrs die rather than eat pork: the law is unchangeable even under torture (6:18–7:42).

T18.note: Individual martyrs (Eleazar, the seven brothers, Razis) and the community are both fully present; one death can serve the nation (7:37–38).

T19.note: Future bodily resurrection "to an everlasting renewal of life" (7:9) at the end of days.

T20.note: Redemptive martyrdom: the brothers hope their deaths end God's wrath on the nation (7:37–38), though they also say "we suffer because of our own sins" (7:32).

conduct.diet: The martyrdom of Eleazar (6:18–31) and the seven brothers (7:1–42) centers on the refusal to eat pork. Eleazar refuses even the pretense of eating it. Diet as covenant identity marker is worth dying for.
conduct.violence_war: War for the Temple and the law is holy. Judas Maccabeus leads with divine support. The suicide of Razis rather than capture (14:37–46) raises questions about the ethics of self-destruction that the book presents approvingly.
conduct.ritual_calendar: The book begins with a letter about Hanukkah (1:1–2:18) and ends with the institution of Nicanor's Day (15:36). Festival commemoration of divine rescue is a governing structure. Proper Temple sacrifice and Sabbath observance are central concerns.

WIS.name: Wisdom of Solomon
WIS.sources: Written in Greek by an Alexandrian Jew; attributed to Solomon as a literary device. Heavily influenced by Middle Platonism and Stoic philosophy while remaining within Jewish monotheism.
WIS.summary: A sophisticated philosophical defense of Jewish wisdom written for Diaspora Jews tempted by Hellenistic culture. Part I argues that righteousness leads to immortality and wickedness to futility (1–5). Part II celebrates Wisdom as a divine emanation whom Solomon courts (6–9). Part III retells the Exodus as a demonstration of how God uses nature to punish idolaters and save the righteous (10–19).

T01.note: The most sustained philosophical attack on idolatry in the tradition (chs. 13–15): idols are dead works of human hands.

T02.note: "You love all things that exist... you spare all things, for they are yours" (11:24–26) — yet Egypt and Canaan are punished.

T03.note: Wisdom "orders all things well" (8:1); God is sovereign and consistent.

T04.note: Strict moral order: "one is punished by the very things by which one sins" (11:16); the righteous attain immortality.

T05.note: Righteousness, not ritual, leads to immortality; the critique of idolatry is moral and philosophical as much as cultic.

T06.note: "Through the devil's envy death entered the world" (2:24) — the first identification of the Eden serpent with the devil; "God did not make death" (1:13).

T07.note: Immortality of the soul: "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God" (3:1–9). Not yet bodily resurrection.

T08.note: Wisdom is a female figure Solomon courts as a bride (8:2), but no human woman has a role.

T09.note: Wisdom is a gift prayed for (8:21; ch. 9), though righteousness is what leads to life.

T10.note: God acts for Israel because of "the oaths and covenants given to our ancestors" (18:22).

T11.note: The wicked "summoned death" by their own words and deeds (1:16); moral choice determines the soul's fate.

T13.note: Addressed to kings, who are accountable to wisdom (6:1–11); Solomon is the model royal sage.

T14.note: Israel is God's children, protected while Egypt is punished; their trials are fatherly testing (11:9–10).

T15.note: Creation fights for the righteous against the wicked (5:17–23; 16:17), but God is merciful to all (11:23).

T16.note: Pseudonymous Solomon; the Exodus is retold typologically and Wisdom personified allegorically.

T17.note: "The imperishable light of the law was to be given to the world" (18:4).

T18.note: Individual souls and their immortality are central.

T19.note: Immortality is already the present state of the righteous (3:1), but a judgment scene follows (ch. 5).

T20.note: The suffering of the righteous only seems like punishment: God tested them "like gold in the furnace" (3:5–6).

conduct.diet: Not addressed. The focus is on moral and spiritual purity rather than food laws.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Solomon's relationship with Wisdom is described in erotic marital terms (8:2–9), sublimating sexuality into the pursuit of divine wisdom. Sexual immorality is listed among the corrupting effects of idolatry (14:12, 24–26).
conduct.homosexuality: Idolatry is linked to sexual disorder including 'confusion of sex' (14:26) among its corrupting effects — a brief but negative reference in the context of condemning idolatry's moral consequences.
conduct.economic_justice: The wicked oppress the righteous poor man, reasoning that might makes right (2:10–20). The book treats this as the defining characteristic of wickedness, and justice for the oppressed as the mark of righteousness.
conduct.violence_war: The Exodus plagues are retold as God's precision instrument: the same phenomena that destroy Egypt protect Israel (16–19). Divine violence in history is celebrated as just and calibrated.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Not specifically addressed. The book's concerns are philosophical and ethical rather than liturgical.

SIR.name: Sirach
SIR.dating: c. 180 BCE (original Hebrew); c. 132 BCE (Greek translation by author's grandson)
SIR.sources: Written in Hebrew by Jesus ben Sira, a Jerusalem scribe and teacher. One of the few Apocryphal books whose author is known. Hebrew manuscripts recovered from Cairo Geniza and Qumran.
SIR.summary: The longest wisdom book in the Jewish tradition, Ben Sira's compendium covers the fear of the Lord, creation, social ethics, proper speech, table manners, friendship, the duties of priests and kings, the beauty of the cosmos, and the Praise of Famous Men (44–50) culminating in the high priest Simon II. Wisdom is identified with Torah (24:23). Deeply indebted to Proverbs while more systematic.

T01.note: Strict monotheism; God is the source of all wisdom: "He is the all" (43:27).

T02.note: Wisdom was given to dwell in Israel (24:8–12), yet "the compassion of the Lord is for every living thing" (18:13).

T03.note: God knows everything and his works are unchanging (42:18–21).

T04.note: Retributive wisdom ethic: good and bad actions reliably produce good and bad consequences in this life.

T05.note: Equal commitment to sacrifice and priestly order (chs. 45, 50) and to social ethics (almsgiving, workers, the poor).

T06.note: "Do not say, 'It was the Lord's doing that I fell away'" (15:11–20) — yet "good and bad, life and death... come from the Lord" (11:14). Sin began with a woman (25:24).

T07.note: Hades ends everything: "in Hades no one asks how long you lived" (41:4); the dead cannot praise (17:27–28).

T08.note: Among the most misogynist texts in the tradition: "Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good" (42:14); warnings about wives and daughters (25:13–26:27; 42:9–14).

T09.note: The fear of the Lord is shown in deeds: almsgiving atones for sin (3:30), honoring parents, keeping the commandments.

T10.note: Everlasting covenants with Phinehas and David (45:24–25; 47:11), but blessing follows obedience.

T11.note: "If you choose, you can keep the commandments" (15:15–17) — though humans are also clay in the potter's hand (33:13).

T12.note: The Temple liturgy under the high priest Simon II is the book's climax (ch. 50).

T13.note: Aaron receives more praise than Moses (ch. 45), and the Praise of Famous Men culminates in a high priest.

T14.note: Wisdom made her home in Israel as its inheritance (24:8–12).

T15.note: The Lord is "compassionate and merciful" (2:11), but the prayer of ch. 36 asks him to "crush the heads of hostile rulers".

T16.note: Practical observation, hymns and a review of Israel's history (chs. 44–50).

T17.note: Wisdom is identified with "the law that Moses commanded us" (24:23) — fixed and eternal.

T18.note: Mostly individual moral formation and self-discipline.

T19.note: Notably this-worldly, though ch. 36 prays for the gathering of the tribes.

T20.note: Suffering is discipline and testing: "gold is tested in the fire" (2:1–6); not simple retribution.

conduct.diet: Ben Sira addresses table manners and moderation extensively (31:12–32:13): don't gorge yourself, be considerate of others at table, wine in moderation. Dietary laws assumed but the focus is on social etiquette.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: Marriage to a good wife is praised as God's gift (26:1–4, 13–16), but the text is deeply suspicious of women. Men are warned against wayward wives (25:13–26), seductive women, and daughters who bring shame. Endogamy is preferred. The text's view of women as sources of danger to men is one of the most negative in Scripture.
conduct.slavery: Ben Sira addresses masters directly (33:25–33): slaves should be given food, discipline, and hard work. 'Fodder and a stick and burdens for a donkey; bread and discipline and work for a slave.' Slavery is assumed as normal and the master's authority is affirmed without question.
conduct.clothing: Not specifically addressed as an ethical matter.
conduct.agriculture: Agricultural imagery pervades the book, but it is used as metaphor rather than as subject of legislation. Tilling the soil is honored as honest work (7:15).
conduct.economic_justice: Extensive teaching: give alms to the poor (3:30–4:10); lend without expecting repayment from the needy (29:1–2); warn against stinginess (14:3–10). Merchants and traders are warned they can hardly avoid sin (26:29–27:3). One of the strongest economic justice sections in the Apocrypha.
conduct.violence_war: The Praise of the Fathers honors military heroes: Joshua who 'waged the wars of the Lord' (46:1), David, and others. War in service of Israel and God's honor is celebrated alongside priestly and prophetic service.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Extensive coverage: proper sacrifice and priestly duty (chapters 45, 50), the beauty of the high priest Simon's liturgy (50:1–21), tithes, offerings, and feast days. Ben Sira is a temple-enthusiast — the cult is one of creation's glories.

BAR.name: Baruch
BAR.sources: Attributed to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, but clearly post-exilic composition. Three distinct sections by possibly different authors: prose confession (1:1–3:8), wisdom poem (3:9–4:4), poems of consolation (4:5–5:9).
BAR.summary: A composite work in three movements: a communal confession of sin explaining the exile as punishment for abandoning Torah; a wisdom poem identifying Wisdom with the Torah given to Israel alone; and lyrical poems of consolation promising Israel's return from exile. The whole addresses Diaspora communities seeking meaning in displacement.

T01.note: "This is our God; no other can be compared to him" (3:35); the nations' gods are nothing.

T02.note: Wisdom/Torah is Israel's alone: "she has not been heard of in Canaan or seen in Teman" (3:22).

T03.note: God is sovereign over history; Babylon is the instrument of his judgment.

T04.note: "The Lord our God is in the right, but there is open shame on us today" (1:15; 2:6): the exile is just.

T05.note: Confession and offerings sent to the Jerusalem altar (1:10) alongside a call to walk in Wisdom's way.

T06.note: "The Lord has kept the calamity ready and brought it upon us" (2:9).

T07.note: "The dead who are in Hades... will not ascribe glory" (2:17); the "everlasting joy" promised is national restoration (4:23, 29).

T08.note: Jerusalem is personified as a widowed mother lamenting her children (4:9–29) — a female voice, but as metaphor.

T09.note: Return to Torah observance — obedience to the written commandments — is the response to exile.

T10.note: The Deuteronomic curses have been fulfilled (1:20), but God promises "an everlasting covenant" on return (2:35).

T11.note: The community can choose repentance and return to God.

T12.note: Money is sent from exile for offerings on the Jerusalem altar (1:10–14).

T13.note: The exiles pray for Nebuchadnezzar's life (1:11) and send to the priest Jehoiakim; no prophet speaks.

T14.note: Election as catastrophe: "under the whole heaven there has not been done the like of what he has done in Jerusalem" (2:2).

T15.note: The consolation poems promise God will gather his children (4:36–5:9) after bringing the calamity.

T16.note: Set in Babylon under the name of Jeremiah's scribe; a composite liturgical work.

T17.note: "She is the book of the commandments of God, the law that endures forever" (4:1).

T18.note: Israel as a collective confesses, mourns and hopes; individual voices are absent.

T19.note: The consolation poems promise return and restoration — future-oriented, not yet apocalyptic.

T20.note: The exile is directly attributed to Israel's sin (1:17; 2:6) — suffering as punishment for covenant breach.

conduct.economic_justice: Not specifically addressed. The focus is on covenant fidelity to Torah rather than social ethics.
conduct.violence_war: Not addressed as a direct ethical concern.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Communal confession and liturgical prayer frame the entire book. It was likely composed for use in communal worship during the exile — a liturgical text before it is a theological one.

LJE.name: Letter of Jeremiah
LJE.dating: c. 300 BCE (earliest Apocryphal text; Qumran fragment dated to c. 100 BCE confirms antiquity)
LJE.sources: Purports to be a letter from Jeremiah to exiles in Babylon. Probably composed in Hebrew or Aramaic; the Greek is the surviving form. Counted as Baruch chapter 6 in Catholic tradition.
LJE.summary: A sustained, repetitive polemic against idolatry addressed to Jews in Babylon. The argument is simple and hammered home seventeen times: idols cannot speak, move, save, or act — they are powerless objects made by craftsmen, dressed by women, and worshipped by fools. Therefore do not fear them.

T01.note: The most concentrated anti-idolatry argument in the tradition: idols cannot speak, see, walk or save — "they are not gods; so do not fear them" (refrain).

T02.note: Addressed to Israel in Babylon: do not be seduced by the surrounding culture's gods.

T03.note: The living God is implicitly sovereign, set against powerless idols; he does not act in the text.

T05.note: About which god to worship, not ethics versus ritual.

T08.note: Women appear as cult functionaries treated with contempt: menstruating women touch the sacrifices (v. 29), women by the roads burn bran (v. 43).

T14.note: "Because of the sins you have committed... you will be taken to Babylon" (v. 2).

T16.note: A polemical essay attributed to Jeremiah, with no narrative.

T18.note: A warning addressed to the community collectively.

T20.note: The exile is punishment for the people's sins (v. 2).

conduct.clothing: Idols are dressed by women in fine garments (v. 11) — used as a sign of their impotence (they need humans to dress them).
conduct.ritual_calendar: The idolatrous cult calendar — priests eating sacrifice, women making offerings during menstruation, torches burned before idols — is described and mocked as evidence of the cult's degradation.

PAZ.name: Prayer of Azariah / Song of Three Jews
PAZ.sources: Inserted between Daniel 3:23 and 3:24 in the Greek and Latin versions. Origin probably Hebrew or Aramaic. Two originally independent pieces: Azariah's prayer of communal confession (vv. 1–22) and the three men's hymn of praise from within the furnace (vv. 28–68).
PAZ.summary: Two liturgical additions to Daniel 3. First, Azariah prays from inside the furnace, confessing Israel's sins and asking God to restore the people despite the absence of Temple sacrifice. Second, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego sing a cosmic praise hymn calling all creation — angels, waters, mountains, animals — to bless the Lord.

T01.note: Only the God of Israel is praised; Nebuchadnezzar's idol is the foil.

T02.note: The covenant with the patriarchs frames the prayer, but the hymn calls "all people on earth" to bless the Lord (v. 60).

T03.note: God hears and rescues; "you are just in all you have done" (v. 4).

T04.note: Azariah confesses that every punishment was just: "we have sinned and broken your law" (vv. 4–8).

T05.note: With no Temple or sacrifice, "a contrite heart and a humble spirit" are offered instead (vv. 15–17) — inward over ritual.

T06.note: God himself handed Israel to lawless enemies (v. 9).

T07.note: The hymn calls on "spirits and souls of the righteous" to bless the Lord (v. 64) — a faint hint that the righteous dead persist.

T09.note: The contrite heart is accepted "as though it were burnt offerings" (v. 16) — grace in place of the prescribed deed.

T10.note: "Do not annul your covenant... for the sake of Abraham your beloved" (vv. 11–13).

T12.note: Prayer in a furnace in exile replaces the unavailable Temple sacrifice (v. 15).

T14.note: Election as burden: "we have become fewer than any other nation" because of sin (v. 14).

T15.note: An angel drives the flame out of the furnace (vv. 26–27): God as deliverer.

T16.note: Liturgical additions to the legend of the fiery furnace.

T17.note: Contrition is accepted in place of the sacrifices the law requires (vv. 15–17).

T18.note: Azariah confesses collective sin on behalf of all Israel.

T19.note: Deliverance is immediate and miraculous, not a future hope.

T20.note: Israel's exile is just punishment (vv. 4–8); the three men themselves suffer as faithful victims of persecution.

conduct.ritual_calendar: The prayer explicitly addresses the absence of Temple cult (no burnt offerings, no sacrifice, no place to stand before God) and proposes prayer and a contrite heart as substitutes — a theological innovation that anticipates post-70 CE Jewish prayer theology.

SUS.name: Susanna
SUS.sources: Appears as Daniel chapter 13 in the Vulgate and Catholic Bibles; as a preface to Daniel in the LXX. Probably composed in Hebrew or Aramaic. Qumran has no fragment.
SUS.summary: Two elders spy on the beautiful and pious Susanna as she bathes in her garden, then falsely accuse her of adultery when she refuses their advances. She is condemned to death. The young Daniel intervenes, cross-examines the elders separately, exposes their lie, and has them executed instead. A story about sexual harassment, false testimony, the vindication of the innocent, and divinely given wisdom.

T01.note: Monotheism is assumed; Susanna prays to the "eternal God" (v. 42).

T02.note: The conflict is within the Jewish community — corrupt elders against a faithful woman. Not a Jewish–Gentile tension.

T03.note: "Eternal God, you know what is secret and are aware of all things before they come to be" (v. 42).

T04.note: The innocent is vindicated and the false witnesses suffer the penalty they intended for her (v. 62).

T05.note: Justice for the falsely accused against corrupt authority is the book's entire point.

T06.note: Evil is human: the two elders.

T08.note: Susanna chooses to refuse and to pray (vv. 22–23, 42–43), but she is subject to male authority at every step and must be rescued by a young man.

T09.note: Susanna's righteous refusal and Daniel's intervention together produce justice.

T11.note: "I choose not to do it and to fall into your hands, rather than sin in the sight of the Lord" (v. 23).

T13.note: God stirs up the spirit of a young man (v. 45) to overrule the elders and judges.

T15.note: God saves the innocent who hope in him (v. 60).

T16.note: A folktale and court story attached to Daniel.

T17.note: The law of Moses on false witness is applied (Deut 19:18–19), via Daniel's new method of cross-examination.

T18.note: One woman's case is the focus; the elders are punished individually.

T20.note: Susanna's suffering is explicitly unjust — she is righteous — and awaits correction.

conduct.marriage_sexuality: Susanna is a faithful, beautiful married woman. The elders' lust for her and their attempt to coerce her into adultery — 'Consent to us and lie with us' (v. 20) — are the book's moral crisis. The text presents female sexual virtue as worth dying for and male sexual predation as deserving death.
conduct.slavery: Susanna has maids who are sent away so she can bathe — slavery assumed as normal background.
conduct.clothing: Susanna removes her veils to wash — a moment of vulnerability exploited by the elders. Clothing and modesty are part of the narrative setup.
conduct.violence_war: The elders are stoned to death per the lex talionis for false testimony — judicial violence sanctioned by Torah law.

BEL.name: Bel and the Dragon
BEL.sources: Appears as Daniel chapter 14 in Vulgate/Catholic Bibles and as an appendix in some LXX manuscripts. Origin probably Semitic. Two episodes: Daniel exposes the priests of Bel and then kills the Dragon.
BEL.summary: Two linked tales in which Daniel uses rational investigation to debunk false religion. In the first, he exposes the priests of Bel as frauds who secretly eat the idol's food, by scattering ashes on the floor and revealing their footprints. In the second, he kills the 'dragon' (a large snake worshipped as a god) by feeding it lethal cakes — proving it is a mortal animal, not a god. Daniel is thrown to the lions for his iconoclasm but miraculously fed by Habakkuk.

T01.note: The most sustained rational debunking of idolatry in the Apocrypha: Bel cannot eat; the dragon dies of cakes. "I worship the Lord my God, for he is the living God" (v. 25).

T02.note: Daniel against Babylonian religion, but the king ends by confessing "great are you, O Lord, the God of Daniel" (v. 41).

T03.note: God rescues Daniel from the lions; the truth is mostly uncovered by Daniel's own reasoning.

T04.note: The fraudulent priests are executed and Daniel's accusers are eaten by the lions (v. 42).

T05.note: The ethical-rational imperative to expose false religion dominates.

T08.note: The priests' wives and children appear only as accomplices put to death with them (vv. 15, 21).

T09.note: Daniel's investigation and his faith in the living God are both essential.

T11.note: Human ingenuity — ashes on the floor, lethal cakes — unmasks the fraud.

T13.note: The prophet-sage Daniel defeats the pagan priests and overrules the king.

T14.note: Daniel is thrown to the lions for his fidelity.

T15.note: God preserves and feeds Daniel in the lions' den (vv. 33–39).

T16.note: Legendary: Habakkuk is carried to Babylon by the hair of his head (v. 36).

T18.note: Daniel acts and suffers as an individual.

T20.note: Daniel's ordeal is persecution of the faithful, not punishment.

conduct.diet: Daniel's lethal cakes for the Dragon (pitch, fat, and hair baked together) are a weapon, not food — though the episode exploits the irony of the idol's 'appetite'. The priests' secret eating of Bel's food offering is the core scandal.
conduct.violence_war: Daniel kills the dragon by feeding it a substance that ruptures it — a form of targeted assassination rather than warfare. The priests are executed by the king for their fraud.
conduct.ritual_calendar: The offering of food to Bel daily is the ritual practice exposed as fraudulent. True worship of the living God requires no such feeding.

1ES.name: 1 Esdras
1ES.sources: A Greek compilation paralleling much of 2 Chronicles 35–36, all of Ezra, and Nehemiah 8. Its unique addition is the Story of the Three Guardsmen (3:1–5:6), in which Zerubbabel wins a wisdom contest at Darius's court by arguing that truth is the strongest thing.
1ES.summary: A retelling of Josiah's Passover, the fall of Jerusalem, the return from exile under Cyrus, the rebuilding of the Temple under Zerubbabel, and the Torah reforms of Ezra. The distinctive Story of the Three Guardsmen frames Zerubbabel as a wisdom hero whose praise of truth wins from Darius the permission to rebuild Jerusalem.

T01.note: Monotheism assumed; the Three Guardsmen story crowns Truth, which "endures and is strong forever" (4:38), with near-divine language.

T02.note: Foreign wives and their children are expelled (8:68–9:36); the restoration community is defined by separation.

T03.note: God acts through Persian decrees and Zerubbabel's wisdom; history follows his purpose.

T04.note: Exile was punishment and return is restoration; the pattern holds.

T05.note: Temple restoration and the proper cult drive the narrative, from Josiah's Passover to Ezra's reforms.

T08.note: Foreign wives are expelled by male decision; in the guardsmen's contest, women "rule" kings — as a rhetorical point about power (4:13–32).

T09.note: Obedience to Torah, including the divorce of foreign wives, marks the restored community.

T10.note: Return depends on covenant fidelity; the people confess and separate.

T11.note: Zerubbabel's wisdom and the community's repentance matter; divine orchestration works through them.

T12.note: The rebuilt Jerusalem Temple and its cult are the goal and culmination.

T13.note: Priests, Levites and the priest-scribe Ezra govern the restored community.

T14.note: Restored as a privileged remnant, but under the burden of past sin.

T16.note: Historical narrative, though the Three Guardsmen story is a wisdom tale presented as history.

T17.note: Ezra reads the law publicly as binding written authority (9:37–55).

T18.note: The returning community as a collective is the subject.

T19.note: Partial, this-worldly restoration; no apocalyptic horizon.

T20.note: The exile is the consequence of the people's sin; return is conditioned on fidelity.

conduct.diet: Not specifically addressed beyond general Torah observance.
conduct.marriage_sexuality: The crisis of foreign wives (8:65–9:36) — men of the restored community who have married foreign women must divorce them, sending them away with their children. Endogamy is enforced as the boundary of the covenant community.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Passover celebration under Josiah (1:1–22) and again after the return (7:10–15). The proper celebration of Passover marks the transition points of the community's history. Temple service and the Levitical calendar are restored as the community's defining structure.

MAN.name: Prayer of Manasseh
MAN.sources: Short penitential prayer attributed to Manasseh king of Judah (2 Chr 33:12–13 mentions such a prayer but does not preserve it). Probably composed in Greek. Found in some LXX manuscripts and the Didache.
MAN.summary: Fourteen verses in which Manasseh, the worst king in the Deuteronomistic History, confesses his sins and pleads for God's mercy. The prayer celebrates God as the God of the repentant, whose mercy surpasses the number of sins and who accepts the penitent even after the worst wickedness.

T01.note: Monotheism assumed: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, creator of heaven and earth (vv. 1–4).

T02.note: The covenant God of the patriarchs, but his mercy reaches even the worst sinner.

T03.note: God is "unchanging"; his mercy is "immeasurable and unsearchable" (vv. 6–7).

T04.note: Manasseh's affliction is deserved; mercy overrides strict desert for the repentant.

T05.note: Repentance of the heart, not ritual: "I bend the knee of my heart" (v. 11).

T07.note: "Do not condemn me to the depths of the earth" (v. 13) — Sheol as the fate he hopes to escape.

T09.note: Forgiveness is God's gift to one who has nothing to offer but repentance.

T10.note: God has "appointed repentance for sinners" (v. 8): mercy is available regardless of the sin's size.

T11.note: The whole point is that even the worst sinner can choose to turn and be heard.

T12.note: Pure personal prayer from captivity, with no Temple or priest.

T15.note: A God of the repentant whose compassion exceeds the number of sins (v. 7).

T16.note: A prayer composed for the repentance only reported in 2 Chronicles 33:12–13.

T18.note: Pure individual prayer: Manasseh speaks for himself alone.

T20.note: His captivity is the consequence of his sins — but the point is that it does not exhaust divine mercy.

conduct.ritual_calendar: Not addressed. The prayer is a personal act of contrition, not a liturgical rite.

PS2.name: Psalm 151
PS2.dating: c. 150 BCE (Hebrew Qumran version 11QPsa; Greek canonical form somewhat later)
PS2.sources: Found at Qumran in an expanded Hebrew version (two psalms, 151A and 151B). The Greek LXX version is a condensed adaptation. Describes David's selection over his brothers and defeat of Goliath.
PS2.summary: A brief autobiographical psalm in the voice of David: God chose him, the least of his brothers and a shepherd, over his older, stronger siblings. David made a lyre and harp to praise God. God sent Samuel to anoint him. Then David defeated Goliath and cut off his head — claiming God's victory over the Philistines.

T01.note: God of Israel against the Philistine giant; monotheism assumed.

T02.note: Israel's God chooses Israel's king against the Philistines.

T03.note: God chooses the least of the brothers and sends Samuel to him; David does not seek it.

T04.note: God exalts the humble and gives him victory.

T05.note: God looks past stature and rank — the youngest is chosen.

T09.note: David is chosen by grace, not merit.

T13.note: The prophet anoints, but the subject is royal legitimacy flowing from divine choice.

T14.note: Election as privilege: chosen, anointed and victorious.

T15.note: David kills Goliath and takes his head — violence against Israel's enemy celebrated; but the opening is a shepherd's psalm.

T16.note: A poetic retelling of the David legend.

T18.note: David's individual calling is the entire subject.

conduct.agriculture: David is a shepherd — pastoral life mentioned but not as an ethical subject.
conduct.violence_war: David kills Goliath with a sling and takes his sword, cutting off his head. The violence is presented as God's victory through the humble chosen one. No ethical reflection on the violence itself.

3MA.name: 3 Maccabees
3MA.sources: Despite its name, has nothing to do with the Maccabean revolt. Set in Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator (221–204 BCE). Probably composed in Alexandria. Survives only in Greek.
3MA.summary: Ptolemy IV attempts to force Egyptian Jews to worship Dionysus, then plans to have them all trampled by drunken elephants. In three miraculous reversals, the elephants turn on the soldiers instead of the Jews. The king repents, grants the Jews a festival, and allows them to punish Jewish apostates. A Diaspora tale of divine protection against forced assimilation, with escalating miraculous interventions.

T01.note: The Jews refuse Ptolemy's demand to be enrolled in the cult of Dionysus (2:29–30); only their God is God.

T02.note: One of the most sharply particularist texts in the Apocrypha: Jews who assimilated are executed by their own community (7:10–15).

T03.note: God intervenes three times — angels appear, the elephants turn, the king's heart changes.

T04.note: The persecutors are humiliated and destroyed; the faithful are delivered.

T05.note: Dietary and social distinctiveness marks the Jews as a people worth divine protection.

T06.note: Evil is the king and his court.

T07.note: No afterlife hope; the deliverance is from death in this life.

T08.note: Women and children are among the threatened community, with no individual roles; newly married women are dragged from their chambers (1:18–19; 4:6).

T09.note: Communal prayer and fasting; God's intervention is the result.

T10.note: God protects his people "according to his covenant" despite their hardships (6:15).

T11.note: Divine action overrides every royal decree and determines the outcome.

T12.note: Set in Egypt; prayer in the hippodrome is effective far from Jerusalem, though the story opens with the Temple's defense (ch. 1–2).

T14.note: God's people are protected and the persecutors humiliated.

T15.note: Divine violence — angels and drunken elephants turned on the soldiers — is the mode of deliverance.

T16.note: A historical romance: 500 drunken elephants, three escalating miracles.

T17.note: Torah observance is fixed and non-negotiable.

T18.note: The Jewish community of Egypt as a collective is the subject.

T20.note: The community's suffering is persecution of the faithful, not punishment.

conduct.diet: Jewish dietary distinctiveness is the precipitating issue: Jews refuse to participate in Ptolemy's cult meals (2:31). The text treats dietary separation from Gentile food as a non-negotiable mark of covenant identity.
conduct.violence_war: The intended violence — trampling by elephants — is miraculous redirected by divine intervention. The Jewish apostates are subsequently executed by the community — internal enforcement of communal boundaries.
conduct.ritual_calendar: A festival commemorating the deliverance is instituted (6:30–36), similar to the pattern of Purim and Hanukkah. Communal celebration as memorial of divine rescue.

2ES.name: 2 Esdras
2ES.dating: Core (4 Ezra, chs. 3–14): c. 100 CE. Christian additions (5 Ezra, chs. 1–2; 6 Ezra, chs. 15–16): 2nd–3rd century CE.
2ES.sources: A composite work. The Jewish core (4 Ezra) was written after the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE, probably in Hebrew or Aramaic, preserved in Latin and other translations. It is among the most important Jewish apocalypses alongside 1 Enoch and 4 Baruch.
2ES.summary: Ezra in Babylon wrestles with God through seven visions over whether God is just in allowing Israel's destruction. An angel gives unsatisfying answers. The visions escalate: a mourning woman transforms into the New Jerusalem; an eagle (Rome) is condemned; a man from the sea (the Messiah) defeats the nations; Ezra dictates 94 books including the 24 of Scripture and 70 secret ones. The most sustained theodicy in the biblical tradition, and the bleakest: only a very few will be saved.

T01.note: Strict monotheism assumed; God's sovereignty over Rome and all history is the point.

T02.note: Only very few will be saved — fewer than the lost — and the nations are condemned with most of Israel (8:1–3).

T03.note: God's plan is fixed, but he is hidden: the angel's answers to Ezra's charge of injustice are consistently unsatisfying.

T04.note: The book's question is whether God's justice holds at all: why the evil heart was left in Adam (3:20–22), why it would be better never to have been born (7:116–118). The answers do not settle it.

T05.note: Keeping the law faithfully distinguishes the few who will be saved.

T06.note: Evil is the "evil heart" (cor malignum) within humans since Adam (3:20–26; 7:118), which God did not remove. No Satan figure.

T07.note: Resurrection and judgment: "the earth shall give up those who are asleep in it" (7:32), with paradise and the "pit of torment" (7:36).

T08.note: The mourning woman who becomes Jerusalem is an allegorical figure, not a statement about women.

T09.note: Torah observance is the criterion, but many who keep it still perish.

T10.note: Few are saved because few keep the law; election does not save Israel as a whole.

T11.note: The times are fixed: "he will not move or arouse them until that measure is fulfilled" (4:36–37); the ages run to a set plan.

T13.note: Ezra as visionary prophet restores the scriptures and 70 secret books (ch. 14).

T14.note: Election brings no protection: Zion lies desolate while Babylon/Rome prospers (3:28–36).

T15.note: The man from the sea destroys the nations with fire from his mouth (13:9–11), though he gathers a peaceful multitude.

T16.note: The most symbolically elaborate text in the Apocrypha: the eagle with twelve wings (Rome), the weeping woman who becomes Jerusalem, the man from the sea.

T17.note: Ezra rewrites the lost scriptures by revelation, and 70 hidden books for the wise go beyond the public law (14:44–47).

T18.note: Each individual is judged at death and "no one shall pray for another" on the day of judgment (7:102–105).

T19.note: The most apocalyptically oriented text in the Apocrypha: messianic age, resurrection, judgment, renewal of creation.

T20.note: The righteous suffer in this age for reasons that remain mysterious; their vindication is certain but deferred.

conduct.economic_justice: Not addressed. The book's concerns are entirely eschatological and theodicial.
conduct.violence_war: Apocalyptic warfare at the end of days: the Messiah destroys the nations assembled against him with fire from his mouth (13:10–11). Divine violence at the eschaton is the mode of ultimate justice.
conduct.ritual_calendar: Not specifically addressed. The restoration of the 24 books of Scripture implies a future Torah community, but the book does not specify ritual calendar concerns.
